rows.en: Since we see that the time of Simeon was the time of victory over the Sadducees, there is no doubt that the Pharisees then enacted many things against the Sadducees; and certainly, besides the matters of which it is said expressly that they were enacted to subdue the Sadducees, there are further ordinances and laws whose reason was to make a public demonstration against them, even though this is not mentioned explicitly; and it is very possible that the time of their birth was in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ, when the victory over them took place. Now we know that the opinion of the Sadducees is that the offering of the omer at Passover is "on the morrow of the sabbath" [Leviticus 23:15] literally, that is, on the first day of the week, and accordingly the festival of Atzeret also falls on the first day of the week; and we also know how many ordinances the Pharisees made to show the error of the Sadducees publicly. Therefore perhaps this too is the reason for their ordinance that they enacted: that people should begin to count aloud and publicly from the sixteenth of Nisan, which is "the morrow of the sabbath" according to the opinion of the Pharisees, and should count each and every day, which day it is of the days of the omer, so that there would be a public demonstration of the matter every day against the Sadducees (R. Aaron Jellinek). And this is our sign that this counting had a special reason: we see that in other commandments too the Torah spoke in this language, as in the commandment of the Jubilee, "And thou shalt number unto thee seven sabbaths of years" [Leviticus 25:8], and in the commandment of the woman's separation in the days of her impurity it is said, "then she shall number to herself seven days" [Leviticus 15:28]; and it did not occur to them to say that the Torah's intent was that they should count every week of the years of the Jubilee and each and every day of the seven clean days (Menaḥot 65b, Tosafot; Ran at the end of Pesaḥim). This can only be because in the counting of the days of the seven weeks between Passover and Atzeret there was a special reason, namely to make a public demonstration against the Sadducees.

From these events it follows clearly for us that the testimony of the later sages, that Simeon restored the Torah to its former state (Kiddushin 66), is very trustworthy. For a long time the field of halakhah had lain desolate; the ways of study had changed their sense under the oppression of the Sadducees, and the midrashim of the Torah had gone into chaos and been lost. The Sadducees paved new roads in the statutes of law and justice, but they went a crooked way, for they invented from their own hearts interpretations and laws that the ancients had not imagined. And how much their sages strove to annul the teaching of the Pharisees forever, we may perceive from the fact that their heart prompted them to make a book of laws to stand for all time. Now, since the world had been desolate for a long time, it cannot be denied that most of their traditions from their ancestors had been forgotten and closed off from the eyes of inquiry, and we can easily understand how heavy the labor was for Simeon to restore the matter to its former state! But the strength of his spirit was among his helpers, for he overcame all obstacles, until under his hand the Oral Torah was fruitful and multiplied like a planting. And we see how many statutes and laws in matters of punishment, both capital and monetary, were fixed then, and how many he restored to their former state. And it is a clear matter that many halakhot concerning the Sanhedrin, the laws of testimony, the rules of justice between a man and his fellow, and all matters of punishment that have survived for us in the Mishnah and the baraita are children of that time; and we may even justly say that then they began to establish anew the rules of justice "between blood and blood, between plea and plea" [Deuteronomy 17:8], and for all "matters of controversy within thy gates" [Deuteronomy 17:8]. Had the book of decrees (*Sefer Gezerata*) that the Sadducees composed survived for us, then from this book we could judge the reason for several statutes that the Pharisees founded at that time, just as we know the reason for some of them from what has reached us of the opinions of the Sadducees about them. In the way of midrash of the Torah that Simeon and the Pharisaic sages of his generation went, they did not yet distance themselves from the plain sense of Scripture. And although at that time they used some of the measures by which the Torah is expounded, and we have seen that most of the later midrashim expounded by the aforementioned⚠1 measures depart from the way of the plain sense, we also know, and it will be made known to us further in the coming chapters, that this deviation from the plain sense did not come through the fault of the measures; rather its cause was that those who used the measures sometimes overstepped the limit and went beyond the measure. If we find that Simeon expounded by binyan av, and likewise used the measure of gezerah shavah (above, in the note), every intelligent person will admit that his use of these measures is very proper and that the midrashim he derived through them are sound and good. And the sum of the matter is this: the deviation from the clear plain sense on both sides of the opponents came in the wake of the opposition, as will be made clear before us further. For this emerges explicitly from all the events concerning the disputes between the Pharisees and the Sadducees whose memory has survived for us: that many matters and ordinances were founded with all strength and force, even where no clear proof for them is found in the Torah, only to make a public demonstration against the Sadducees. Were not all the particular things they enacted for the reaping of the omer, such as that they did not hesitate to reap the omer on the Sabbath, and various other customs that they observed in its reaping and its offering (Menaḥot 65a), all prepared and founded only because they saw that the dispute with the Sadducees required it? And indeed we have also seen that the Sadducees on their side followed this same practice of deviating in several religious matters only to oppose the Pharisees. And if someone says to us: "that the Sadducees are the stationary ones, who hold fast to the tradition of the old covenant and to the tradition of the first Scribes, who explained the Torah very plainly and defined the commandments according to the rules of the plain sense and the original intent; and the Pharisees were the movers among the stationary, those who travel on and who widen, in their definition, the ways of performing the commandments in the manner of derash," we too will say that "the witness is a false witness" [Deuteronomy 19:18]. Indeed this witness (the book *Ma'amar ha-Ishut*) perverted the line of justice out of love for the one side and from bias toward the other. But the truth is this: the Pharisees kept the way of tradition and walked in the footsteps of their ancestors. And it was received among them that the heads of the generations are authorized by the Torah to do as they did in expounding the Torah, for this was laid down in the wisdom of the Giver of the Torah: not to give the Torah cut and closed. Therefore even the new interpretations were in their eyes as received ones, and even when they departed from a received interpretation, this was not a departure from tradition but a departure by the power of tradition. Whoever looks at the course of the interpretation of the Torah in every generation and in all the ancient times will know that this view goes on from generation to generation; and therefore, if the Pharisees were the movers, they acted according to the original intent, and so did the prophets and after them the Scribes. But the Sadducees were not the stationary ones. Indeed, at the moment when they kindled the fire of dispute, for one reason or another, both these and those stood at one position in understanding the Torah; and as the division of hearts grew stronger, both these and those were movers: the Pharisees were the movers forward, like their ancestors in every generation, and in this they were the bearers of tradition; and the Sadducees too were movers, but they went backward and not forward, and through this they broke the bonds and distanced themselves from the way of their ancestors entirely. Now the guilt of the Sadducees is great on two sides. On their own side, that they went backward and abandoned the original intent. And in this too their guilt is great, that they caused the Pharisees to be forced at times to go beyond the measure in their midrashim, which was the reason that in the course of time the plain midrash changed the sense it had had from days of old.

rows.en: One thing is told of Simeon ben Shetaḥ which by our views today is a cruel deed. It is this: in his time the daughters of Israel were devoted to the practice of witchcraft, and to cut off this superstition from the land he took action and hanged eighty witch women on a tree in one day, not because they deserved it but because the hour required it (Sanhedrin 46a). But who can judge today a deed done close to two thousand years ago, and who can weigh in the balance of the opinions of our time ancient actions whose causes, which forced their doers to do them, we do not know? At any rate we can know from this that he was not exacting about the letters of the statutes to a hair's breadth, for he knew what the time demanded of him, and he acted according to the demands of the time. We have already seen in the course of our account, and will see further, that this was a great principle among the sages of all generations: to issue rulings for the hour as the hour required them, whether to make a fence for the Torah or for another reason necessary for the welfare of the nation; and from such rulings for the hour there sometimes came forth halakhic consequences that became "a statute which shall not pass" [Psalms 148:6]. We have seen this in the clearest manner in the prohibition, fixed and standing, of fighting on the Sabbath. The Ḥasidim at the beginning of the Hasmonean war gave their lives for it; afterward they permitted it by a ruling for the hour; at various times they went back to treating it as forbidden; and after a time it was permitted entirely. And the outcome of this permission was the principle that they laid down, that the saving of life overrides the Sabbath, and it became a standing halakhah that all the winds cannot move from its place. Simeon ben Shetaḥ and his colleague decreed impurity on the land of the gentiles and on glass vessels (Shabbat 14b); and although these decrees had been founded by Yose ben Yoezer and his colleague, they were nevertheless compelled to found them once again, because from the end of the time of Yoḥanan the High Priest, from the time he turned his mind to follow the Sadducees, these decrees had sunk into oblivion; for they were not permitted to keep the teaching of the Pharisees at all, as Yoḥanan had decreed upon them. And therefore, when Simeon ben Shetaḥ and his colleague came and prevailed over the Sadducees and restored their teaching to its former state, these decrees too were renewed.{v1_08_10:1} A second decree they made concerning the impurity of metal vessels (Shabbat, ibid.). And although the impurity of metal vessels is explicit in the Torah (Numbers 31:22), perhaps in those days they were lax in the matter and treated it as permitted against the law; or they used a stratagem and passed them through fire, and after passing them through fire did not practice immersion in water for them, nor seven days' impurity, but declared them pure at once, since the plain meaning of the words of the Torah as written does not indicate immersion in water and seven days' impurity after passing through fire. At any rate the Sadducees did not admit their impurity, and since the opinion of the Sadducees was rooted in the people, Simeon ben Shetaḥ was compelled to decree impurity upon them. Do we not see that Queen Shelamzion [Salome Alexandra], who cleaved to the customs of the Pharisees, nevertheless thought to remove the vessels that had become impure in her house from their impurity by breaking them, giving them to a smith, and having him weld them (Shabbat 16b)? From this we can judge that even those who followed the Pharisees did not know the conditions and limits of this impurity, because they had neglected it all the days of the Sadducees' rule. And it is possible that according to the Sadducees the intent of the Torah, which speaks of kinds of metal, is not to vessels made of metal but to the raw lumps of the kinds of metal.{v1_08_10:2} However it may be, Simeon and his colleagues were compelled to restore the matter to its place and its limit, and this is what is meant when they said that Simeon made a decree concerning metal vessels. Simeon enacted another great ordinance concerning the woman's ketubbah. He saw in his time that the bond of marriage had grown weak and that it was a light thing in the husband's eyes to divorce his wife, and all the ordinances that had been enacted with regard to the woman's ketubbah had not helped to remove the stumbling block. For at first the custom was that her ketubbah was kept with her parents, and it was easy in his eyes to send her away (for he said to her, "Go to your ketubbah"); and they enacted that her ketubbah be kept with her husband, and even so it was easy in his eyes to send her away (for the ketubbah was ready in his hand at all times). For this they enacted that he should buy with his wife's ketubbah cups, bowls and dishes (and this too did not help, for even then he could say to her, "Take your ketubbah," that is, the vessels that he had bought and that were set aside for her ketubbah); and they enacted that he should do business with his wife's ketubbah, for since he does business with it he loses it (Yerushalmi Ketubbot, end of chapter 8). And after they enacted this, it is self-evident that he was compelled to pledge all his property to her for her ketubbah; and therefore this ordinance is a great obstacle, so that he cannot divorce her lightly; and it is attributed to Simeon ben Shetaḥ.{v1_08_11:1} This ordinance sheds light on matters of divorce in general: for if they said that it was easy in his eyes to send her away, it appears that in ancient times they were accustomed to divorce for any matter and not only for a matter of unchastity, as the House of Shammai wished to establish a law that a man may not divorce his wife unless he has found in her "some unseemly thing" [Deuteronomy 24:1] (Gittin 88b⚠1). He enacted another great ordinance, namely that it should be a duty upon every man in Israel to send the children to school (Yerushalmi Ketubbot, ibid.). And to this ordinance the events of the time without doubt forced him. For during the days when the hand of the Sadducees was uppermost, the schools too were without doubt laid waste. After the decree was issued in the days of Yoḥanan the High Priest to remove the opinions of the Pharisees, the spirit of the Sadducees spread in the school as well. And the good people, especially among the common folk, who always followed the opinions of the Pharisees, refrained from sending their sons to school, and this neglect lasted until the days of Simeon; and therefore there was great necessity to make this ordinance.

rows.en: Further, there have survived for us from Simeon ben Shetaḥ and Judah ben Tabbai precious sayings that warn the judges to be deliberate in judgment, to hold to the measure of justice, to keep far from wrong, from favoritism in judgment and from perverting it, and to be careful in their words in the examination of the witnesses (Avot chapter 1). Of the events of Judah's life nothing remains beyond what has been mentioned; but of Simeon's life several more events are told, all of which show that he acted by the measure of strict justice in all his deeds, as was without doubt fitting for his time. We have seen that he let his son be sentenced to death and fulfilled in himself the principle: "Let the law pierce the mountain." So too the deed with the women in Ashkelon shows it, whom he sentenced to death, hanging eighty in one day against the fine points of the law because of the needs of the hour. A trustworthy proof of his love of justice and uprightness in all his affairs is given us by an incident that happened to him with an Ishmaelite. Simeon bought a donkey from an Ishmaelite for its full price; and when they brought it to his house, his disciples found a precious stone hanging on its neck, and they said to Simeon: "Our master, 'the blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich'!" [Proverbs 10:22]. He answered them and said: "A donkey I bought; a precious stone I did not buy." He went and returned it to the Ishmaelite, and that Ishmaelite proclaimed over him: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Simeon ben Shetaḥ" (Deuteronomy Rabbah, Ekev). We see from this that the measure of justice was his measure; and even though his lot did not fall in the pleasantness of wealth, for he made a meager living and was compelled to trade in flax (Yerushalmi Bava Metzia 2:5), he was not tempted on that account to "get riches, and not by right" [Jeremiah 17:11], and he dealt justly even with a man of another religion. In beliefs and opinions his thought was pure, and he did not go beyond the measure in piety. In his days there lived a man who was held by the people to be practiced in miracles; this man was called Ḥoni the Circle-Maker. Once there was famine in the land for three years, and when most of Adar had passed without rain they sent to him, saying: "Pray, that rain may fall." He said to them: "Bring in the Passover ovens, so that they do not dissolve"; and he prayed, and no rain fell. He drew a circle and stood within it and said before Him: "Master of the world, Your children have turned their faces to me, for I am like a son of the house before You. I swear by Your great name that I will not move from here until You have mercy on Your children." The rains began to drip. He said: "Not thus did I ask." They came down in fury. He said: "Not thus did I ask," until they fell properly. . . . Simeon ben Shetaḥ sent to him: "You deserve to be excommunicated" (Ta'anit 19a; and see the Yerushalmi and *Megillat Ta'anit* chapter 18⚠1). For Simeon could not restrain himself when one "formed out of the clay" [Job 33:6] spoke thus toward God; and Simeon was zealous against him especially because he believed in himself that he had the power to compel his Creator by his prayer to do his will, and caused the people too to believe so, which in Simeon's view is not so, as the words put in his mouth show: "Had a decree been decreed as it was decreed in the days of Elijah, would you not have brought the many to the desecration of the Name?" From these brief words we learn that in his view the prayer of the righteous does not avail against the divine decree. And therefore, if a decree has been decreed as in the days of Elijah, there is no power in man's prayer to turn back the decree; but for the common people he would thereby cause great harm to their faith. For Ḥoni showed in his words that it was certain that his request would be done in any case, and thereby he strengthened the people's expectation that his prayer would certainly help; yet perhaps a decree had been decreed and the prayer would not help, and what would be the end of these things? A weakening of faith, and the name of Heaven would be desecrated. "These are the edges of his ways" [Job 26:14]. When did Simeon die? It has not been made known to us. Nor do we know how long he lived after the death of Queen Shelamzion, who conducted the government according to the counsel of the Pharisees for nine years.

rows.en: The great events that occurred in the time of Simeon necessarily brought a new spirit into the ways of study of the Pharisees. From now on they were compelled to widen the ways of midrash of the Torah in order to give the opinions of the Pharisees a foundation and a root in the Torah of Moses; and even more they were compelled to hem in the laws of the Sadducees, which had been rooted in the nation for many years, and to bring proofs against them from the written Torah. To achieve this purpose, several measures and rules of midrash were of great use to them, for these measures by their nature have the power of expansion; they are fitting means to widen the midrash of the Torah according to the understanding of the Pharisees and their traditions, as indeed the measures widened from generation to generation. And already in the first generation after the death of Simeon ben Shetaḥ and Judah ben Tabbai their disciples arose and occupied themselves much with the midrash of the Torah according to the measures, until they acquired among the people the honored name "great expounders," as will be explained before us in the next chapter.
Shemaiah, Avtalyon. — The Sons of Bathyra. —

When Shelamzion died, the good fortune of the nation died with her. A great quarrel broke out between her sons, Yoḥanan Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, over the throne of the kingdom. Aristobulus prevailed over his brother, and in the end they came to terms. Yoḥanan withdrew his hand from all affairs of the kingdom, and the government came to Aristobulus. Hyrcanus had a friend named Antipater the Idumean. He was a foreigner by birth, and he had become a Jew at the time when Yoḥanan the First compelled the Idumeans to enter the religion of the Jews. He sowed strife between the brothers and enticed Yoḥanan to flee with him secretly from Jerusalem and to conspire against Aristobulus. For Antipater was cunning and in all his deeds turned to his own gain, and he saw an advantage for his gain in thrusting Aristobulus from his position and turning the kingdom over to Yoḥanan, since he knew well that if Yoḥanan reigned he would be king only in appearance, for Yoḥanan was a man of weak spirit, and he would be in Antipater's hand "as the clay in the potter's hand" [Jeremiah 18:6]. And indeed Antipater's desire prospered in his hand. Yoḥanan, from weakness of spirit, was enticed by him. Many of the Jews who were rebelling against their lord Aristobulus gathered to them and conspired against the government; the Arab king also joined them, and they went up against Jerusalem and besieged it (*Antiquities* 14:1⚠1). Aristobulus and the priests who were inside asked their brothers who were besieging them not to prevent them from offering the obligatory sacrifices to the Lord, and to send them lambs every day, and they would gladly pay them for these in full silver. The Jews besieging them agreed to this request. The priests let down to them from the top of the wall a basket full of denarii every day, and they would send up to them the daily offerings. But there was among the besiegers an old man, a man of evil deeds, and he spoke to the men of war in Greek and incited them not to do so, saying: "As long as they are occupied with the service of the sacrifices, they will not be delivered into your hands." And without doubt this old man thought that if they were compelled to cancel the service of the sacrifices, they would thereby be won over, or be compelled to surrender to them. The next day they let down denarii to them in the basket as every day, but they sent up to them not lambs but two pigs. And on that day there was a great earthquake in all the Land of Israel, and all the fruits of the land were destroyed (Josephus, ibid.; and see Graetz vol. 3, 538); and the people said that this had come upon them because of the great outrage that the besieging Jews had committed, desecrating the Name and the service of the Temple. This event was the cause of several ordinances. At that hour they said: "Cursed be the man who raises pigs, and cursed be he who teaches his son Greek wisdom."{v1_08_13:1} Because of the event in which they refused to let down lambs to them for the daily offerings, and they were compelled to provide daily offerings from another place, a new ordinance was founded, that the daily offering is offered within four hours (Yerushalmi Berakhot 4:1). Likewise, all the days on which they let down lambs to them for the daily offerings, they offered them even though they had not been inspected four days before their offering; yet according to the law of the Talmud the inspection was necessary, so that without it the sacrifice is disqualified (Sifra, Vayikra, section 3; Pesaḥim 96a; Tosefta ibid. chapter 5; Sukkah chapter 5; Sukkah 42b). From this too we learn that not all the consequences that the sages of the Mishnah and the midrash drew at a late time were held so in practice in an early time. So too they departed from their custom regarding the bringing of the omer. For the commandment of the omer is to bring it from nearby, and it appears that they were exacting in this commandment, and there was a weighty reason in the matter to bring it only from nearby and not from afar: for they wanted to perform the reaping of the omer publicly because of the dispute of the Sadducees (Menaḥot 65a); but such publicity is possible only near Jerusalem and without a long interval between the reaping and the bringing. And at that time, when there was blight because of the great storm and they had no new grain to bring from nearby, they did not hesitate and brought it from afar, from Gaggot Tzerifin, and the two loaves at Atzeret from the valley of Ein Sokher (Menaḥot 64b; Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:1). This event was around the days of the festival of Passover, and they had no Passover offerings to offer (Josephus, ibid.). But the end of the quarrel was evil for Israel, and at that time they lost their freedom, never to return. For the warring brothers both turned to the Roman governors in Asia and called on Pompey, the commander of the Roman armies, who at that time was with his forces in the provinces near the land of Judah, and they asked him to make a settlement between the brothers; but the end of his settlement was to rob both of them of the government, and Israel "became a servant under tribute" [Genesis 49:15] to Rome. He set up Yoḥanan Hyrcanus as High Priest and Nasi in Israel, and Antipater was his second-in-command and overseer of the whole land, and in his hand were all the affairs of government. Even after the death of Pompey, when Julius Caesar came in his place, the matter did not change; for Caesar too showed him favor, and Antipater did in the land of Judah whatever was right in his eyes. He had four sons, whom he made governors of the provinces. Phasael the firstborn he set up as governor in Jerusalem, and his second son Herod as governor in the land of Galilee. Yoḥanan Hyrcanus was a man who walked in his innocence and was weak of understanding, and with a willing soul he left all the affairs of government in Antipater's hand, for he loved quiet; but his sloth brought it about that before long he was pushed aside by the times. His eyes were too dim to see that deceit, cunning and schemes were encamped around him and were among those who passed by him⚠2. If Antipater strove to rule over Yoḥanan's spirit, Herod was even worse than his father, for he lay in wait for Yoḥanan in secret to push him from his position and to raise himself to the kingship in his place. By his cleverness and his many schemes he won the favor of the Romans, until by scheming and bribery he reached the throne of the kingdom. With these events many troubles came upon Israel. Desecration of the holy, shedding of innocent blood, oppression, violence and robbery passed and swept through Judah like "an overflowing scourge" [Isaiah 28:15]. No one can tell how many were the hardships that came upon them in those days, from the hand of Pompey and his legions and from the hand of the Roman governors who came time after time to rule in the land of Judah. As in the days of Aristobulus only trouble and sorrow found the Jews, so it was also a short time after this, in the days when Alexander, the firstborn son of Aristobulus, rose up to turn the kingdom to himself. His desire did not prosper and "his latter end shall come to destruction" [Numbers 24:20]; but through the events that caused his downfall the cup of poison passed over the people too. The days after that, when Antigonus, the second son of Aristobulus, rose up, were also no better than these. Antigonus conspired against Yoḥanan and made a covenant with the Persians, and with their help defeated Yoḥanan, and they led him captive to Babylon. But his kingdom too did not endure, for after three years had passed Herod came, aided by the Romans with a heavy force, and besieged Jerusalem and took it, and then the government passed into the hand of Herod. All these wars and quarrels were a curse in the midst of Israel. Yet in all these events our eyes behold one wondrous sight: all the heart-rending hardships that came upon them did not bring an end to the study of the Torah. More than thirty years passed from the beginning of the brothers' quarrel until Herod came, conquered the land and ascended the throne of the kingdom. All these years were years of toil and hardship, and yet in the midst of these events the houses of study of the sages were not laid waste and the Sanhedrin did not cease; and this is a proof that the men who stood at the head of the Sanhedrin knew and understood what such a time demanded of them. And truly so it was. If we consider the character of the two sages who were the heads of the Torah and of the Sanhedrin at that time, and pay attention to the course of their opinions and their qualities, and especially to their teachings, then we shall find that it is no wonder that all the events of the time did not bring great harm to the study of the Torah.

footnotes.en: See on this Bavli Shabbat (14b), and the Yerushalmi there and in Pesaḥim, end of chapter 1; and in the Yerushalmi Shabbat it is decided that Simeon ben Shetaḥ again founded the decree.

We have already said that the traces of the opinions of the Sadducees are embedded in the midrashim of the Pharisees. For the most part they are found in the salka da'ta ("it might have entered your mind") of the midrashim, when the author of the midrash says "one might think," or "it is not so," and similar expressions. Therefore it is possible that the opinion of the Sadducees was that when the Torah said "Only the silver and the gold, etc." [Numbers 31:22], the intent is not to vessels but to raw lumps of metal. And there is a hint of the matter in Sifrei, portion Mattot, section 158: "Only the gold, etc.: vessels" (so the reading in the edition of R. Meir Friedmann, following the reading of a manuscript); "you say vessels, or does it mean only raw lumps? Behold, you reason, etc." And therefore this salka da'ta is perhaps the interpretation of the Sadducees, and the Pharisees said that it is not so, but that the impurity of vessels is learned by an a fortiori argument. And according to the Tosefta Kelim Bava Metzia chapter 2, Tosefta Ḥullin chapter 1 and the Bavli there (25a), raw metal vessels are pure and raw wooden vessels are impure; and it seems to me that the root of this halakhah too lies in the reason I have written, that the opinion of the Sadducees was that the verse "Only the silver, etc." refers to the raw lumps; therefore they changed⚠1 the law of raw metal vessels deliberately, declaring them pure against the opinion of the Sadducees.

footnotes.en: So, it seems to me, is the sense of the baraita in the Yerushalmi, which agrees with the baraita in the Bavli. And it is clear that the last ordinance was that the husband should do business with it; and since he does business with her ketubbah, there is no longer anything set aside for her ketubbah, and of necessity he must pledge all his property to her and write for her: "All the property I have is surety and guarantee for the ketubbah"; and this is also the sense of the Tosefta, chapter 12. And I have seen that the scholar Graetz, 533, emended the text of the Yerushalmi and read thus: "At first her ketubbah was deposited with her parents, and it was easy in his eyes to divorce her; they enacted that her ketubbah be with her husband — and they enacted that a man should buy with his wife's ketubbah cups, bowls and dishes of silver and gold (?), and still, when he was angry with her, he would say to her, 'Take your ketubbah'; and therefore they went back and enacted that a man should do business with his wife's ketubbah, until Simeon ben Shetaḥ came and enacted that he should write for her: 'All my property is surety for her ketubbah.'" This implies that already before Simeon they enacted that he do business with her ketubbah, and afterward Simeon enacted that he write "all my property, etc." But this is not so, for it is impossible to enact that he do business with her ketubbah unless he pledges his property to her, as is known to every student of the Talmud; and in the Tosefta too it is explicit that her ketubbah should be with her husband (that is, that he should do business with it) and that he should write, etc. — all of it the ordinance of Simeon; and in the Yerushalmi they said explicitly that Simeon enacted that he do business with her ketubbah. Therefore there is no room for Graetz's emendation, and the words of the Yerushalmi need no emendation, only explanation.
